doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Nat's Basic Black Band breaks up; Woody Shaw's band and Rosewood
summary: The band tires of road duties; Woody Shaw recruits him, he arranges Rosewood, and Shaw later fires him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: and the Basic Black Band. Because Nat didn’t feel like doing all the road work, all the little stuff like the renting of the truck and all this kind of stuff. So he put that in our laps. But we got tired of it after a while. So that’s when he disbanded as a band, realizing he had to come back on board and take charge. Because we liked it for a while, and then we got kind of tired of it so we went to Nat and said listen, can we have a talk? So we had a band meeting. And that’s when he decided I’m going to dismantle this band. But I was at a club and Woody Shaw was in the club. He had a way of talking, oh this gruff little voice. And he says, “You want to join my band?” “What?” “You want to join my band?” I loved him as a player, because he was one of the baddest cats. But I wasn’t too crazy about him, you know, I wasn’t sure I wanted to work with him you know. So I said, “Well who else is in the band?” So he says, “Well Victor Lewis is on drums, and Carter Jefferson is on tenor and Clint Houston.” “Cool, yeah, okay.” I loved those guys, so if nothing else I’ll have some great cats to work with, if I can’t even stand Woody. But it turned out to be one of the most incredible experiences. And Woody became a friend as the years progressed, only maybe two years. During that time Woody had done an interview and commented about the members of the band. And it got to me. And he said, “You know Onaje is to me as Gil Evans is to Miles.” I said oh, oh, okay. I still have to find that article, because I lost it somewhere. It was a DownBeat on microfilm or whatever. But the other thing that really blew my mind is when he got the deal with Columbia Records. And he was going to do an album called “Rosewood.” And he said “Onaje, I want you to arrange this tune. Just do it.” Okay. So I took it upon myself to arrange a tune, no running interference, I didn’t have to show him what I did to get his approval, I just did the tune. And it was like the title track of his first major deal, Columbia Records. I didn’t put it together. Rosewood. You know it’s like a tree or something like that? Later on down the line it turned out that it was a song that was dedicated to his parents. Because his mother’s name is Rose and his father’s name was Woody. So Rose-Wood. And I felt really honored. Because this is something, this is an homage to your parents, who gave birth to you, and you want somebody that’s not in the family, to actually bring your sentiments to your parents alive. Wow man. I mean still to this day it’s something that really touches me as far as the confidence he had in me and the faith he had in me to bring it through. The break-up of the band was hard, or him firing me was difficult here but I was able to handle it so to speak. Because he called me up one day and says, “I think you forgot who the leader of the band is, I don’t like your attitude, and I want my music back. You got anything to say?” “No.” Nothing. And that was it. And a few years later we hooked up again, because it couldn’t last, because we had some history. And I guess the unfortunate thing of that whole thing was that two of the members or three of the members are gone now. Three out of the five. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-
